title: Vulcan, the planet that wasn’t there

paragraphs.text: The discovery of the seventh planet in the Solar System, Uranus, in 1781 was a major astronomical breakthrough. Those involved in observing this distant planet and plotting its slow 84-year movement around the Sun were at the cutting edge of science at that time. However, as the decades passed, astronomers found that Uranus was deviating slightly from where it ought to be. This was a mystery, as by the early nineteenth century astronomers were confident that they fully understood both gravity and planetary orbits. Some speculated that Uranus was being pulled from its expected position by the gravitational field of some unseen body, possibly an eighth planet.

In the early 1840s the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier carried out a series of painstaking calculations, analysing the orbit of Uranus in order to determine the precise nature of the possible new planet’s effect on it. By 1846, Le Verrier had completed his work, which showed that the new planet should lie between the constellations of Aquarius and Capricorn. Many scientists took little interest in his claims, perhaps because his reasoning and conclusions were considered unconventional. However, having received a letter from Le Verrier, German astronomer Johann Galle and his team set about using the Frenchman’s calculations to locate the theoretical body, and confirmed the existence of the planet Neptune on 23 September 1846. It was within one degree of the position Le Verrier had predicted. The fact that Galle and Le Verrier took all the credit for this discovery is controversial because in 1843, the astronomer John Couch Adams had also calculated that Uranus was being influenced by an undiscovered eighth planet. However, recent research suggests his work was significantly less comprehensive than Le Verrier’s.

Encouraged by his success, Le Verrier investigated the inner Solar System, and in particular Mercury, the closest planet to the sun, because there was a similar mystery to solve. Mercury’s distance from the Sun varies from the closest point, when it is 46 million kilometres from the Sun, and the furthest point, when the distance is 70 million kilometres. This was in accordance with the laws of planetary motion known at the time. However, scientists had noticed that sometimes Mercury wasn’t in the location it was expected to be. The orbits of all the other planets could be predicted perfectly, but it was unclear why Mercury was an exception to this rule. The problem was that Mercury often reached its closest point to the Sun earlier than expected, and its most distant point later than predicted although the differences were tiny.

Le Verrier was determined to prove that Mercury’s irregular orbit was not due to the gravitational pulls of Venus, Earth or Mars. He became convinced that a previously unseen planet between Mercury and the Sun must be responsible. Since this planet would be smaller than Mercury and extremely close to the Sun, it would be difficult to see. Le Verrier said that the ideal chance to spot it would be when total eclipses of the Sun are occurring.

In 1859 Le Verrier published his calculations and proposed that once it was located the planet should take the name of Vulcan, the god of fire in Roman mythology. This was because of its proximity to the Sun. Not long after, Vulcan was apparently discovered during an astronomical phenomenon known as a transit, which is when a planet passes across the surface of the Sun as seen from Earth. The man responsible was a doctor, Edmond Lescarbault, who was not a professional astronomer and worked from an observatory in his garden. He hadn’t intended to hunt for a new planet as he was focused on searching for sunspots, small, dark, cool patches that appear on the Sun’s surface. He didn’t even note how long Vulcan took to cross the Sun as he didn’t own a reliable watch with a second hand.

Le Verrier had some doubts because of the small size of this supposed planet, and believed that it was probably too small to account for the irregularities of Mercury’s orbit. But Le Verrier eventually overcame his initial scepticism and Vulcan’s discovery was formally announced in March 1860.

Within weeks astronomers were pointing out that the body ‘seen’ by Lescarbault would be quite prominent, so it was unlikely to have been missed by other observers with superior equipment. Most other astronomers who used Le Verrier’s figures to locate Vulcan failed to do so. Those who did report it claimed positions that didn’t match with the supposed orbit. Vulcan was spotted occasionally over the next 40 years, sometimes by very reliable observers, but by 1900 its existence was thought to be highly improbable. Photography had by then revolutionised astronomy, yet not a single image had captured the tiny planet. The problem of Mercury’s orbit was therefore unsolved.

In 1915 Albert Einstein published his ground-breaking General Theory of Relativity. This put forward the idea that space and time were linked, and that very large objects could bend both Einstein was showing that there was more going on in extreme gravitational fields than previously thought. Applying his reasoning to Mercury’s orbit, Einstein showed that at its closest point to the Sun, Mercury was moving through space that was being ‘bent’ by the Sun’s gravity, effectively lengthening the distance Mercury was travelling by a tiny amount. This theory solved the mystery of why scientists couldn’t always precisely locate Mercury’s position.
